spot.title: Bragg angle of the (100) reflection
spot.intro: A simple cubic crystal with lattice constant $a=4.0$ Å is hit by Cu K$\alpha$ X-rays, $\lambda=1.54$ Å. Find the Bragg angle $\theta$ of the first (100) peak.
steps: Laue condition for elastic scattering: $\mathbf k'-\mathbf k=\mathbf G$, with $|\mathbf k|=|\mathbf k'|=2\pi/\lambda$.
The peak appears at a detector angle $2\theta\approx45.3^\circ$.
spot.why: Bragg's law is $2d\sin\theta=n\lambda$. The factor 2 comes from $|\mathbf G|=2k\sin\theta$ (the scattering vector is $2k\sin\theta$ long), i.e. the path difference between neighbouring planes is $2d\sin\theta$.

source.where: adapted from Problem 1 (Bragg/reciprocal lattice), topic: Laue condition vs Bragg law

spot.title: Fermi energy at $n=5.00\cdot10^{22}\,\text{cm}^{-3}$
spot.intro: Free electron gas in 3D with $n=5.00\cdot10^{22}\,\text{cm}^{-3}$. Compute $k_F$ and $E_F$.
steps: States in k-space: one k-point occupies $(2\pi)^3/V$, and the Fermi sphere has volume $\tfrac{4\pi}{3}k_F^3$.
spot.why: Every k-point holds two electrons (spin up and down), so $N=2\cdot\frac{4\pi k_F^3/3}{(2\pi)^3/V}$. The spin factor 2 was forgotten, which gives $6\pi^2$ instead of $3\pi^2$ and an $E_F$ too large by $2^{2/3}$.

source.where: adapted from MC (m) Fermi energy of 5.00e22 cm^-3, topic: spin factor in k_F

spot.title: Mean energy per electron at $T=0$
spot.intro: Show that the mean kinetic energy per electron of a 3D free Fermi gas at $T=0$ is $\tfrac35E_F$.
steps: Density of states $g(E)=C\sqrt E$ with $C$ constant, filled up to $E_F$.
Compare with the known result $\tfrac35E_F$: the discrepancy means the integration must be rechecked.
spot.why: $\int E^{3/2}dE=\tfrac{2}{5}E^{5/2}$, not $\tfrac23E^{5/2}$: the exponent after integration is $3/2+1=5/2$, and the prefactor is the inverse of this exponent, $2/5$.

source.where: adapted from the script, free electron gas (Sommerfeld), topic: ground-state energy

spot.title: Debye temperature of a monatomic solid
spot.intro: A monatomic solid has $N/V=6\cdot10^{28}\,\text{m}^{-3}$ atoms and a mean sound velocity $v=3000$ m/s. Determine the Debye temperature $\Theta_D$.
steps: Debye model: linear dispersion $\omega=vk$ for all three branches, cut at $k_D$.
Each branch has exactly $N$ allowed k-values in the first Brillouin zone.
Take instead the total mode count in one cut: $\frac{4\pi k_D^3/3}{(2\pi)^3/V}=3N$, so $k_D=(18\pi^2N/V)^{1/3}$.
spot.why: The 3 polarisations are already used in step 3 (each branch contains $N$ modes). Step 4 counts the factor 3 a second time with a single sphere and mixes up per-branch and total mode number.

source.where: Ch. 2.3-2.4 (pp. 52-65), topic: Debye model, adapted numbers

spot.title: Zone-boundary frequencies of the diatomic chain
spot.intro: Linear chain with masses $m<M$ alternating, nearest-neighbour spring constant $C$, lattice constant $a$ (two atoms per cell). Find the frequencies at $q=\pi/a$.
steps: At $q=\pi/a$ the right-hand side vanishes, so $\omega^2=2C/m$ or $\omega^2=2C/M$.
Since $m<M$, $2C/m>2C/M$, so the optical branch has $\omega_{opt}=\sqrt{2C/m}$ (upper).
The acoustic branch at the boundary is therefore $\omega_{ac}=\sqrt{2C/m}$ as well, and the gap closes.
spot.why: The two roots are different: the larger one belongs to the optical branch, the smaller one to the acoustic branch. The acoustic mode at the boundary is $\sqrt{2C/M}$ (heavy atoms move, light atoms at rest), so a gap of width $\sqrt{2C/m}-\sqrt{2C/M}$ exists.

source.where: Ch. 2.2.5 (pp. 45-48), topic: diatomic chain, zone boundary

spot.title: Sign of the Hall field for electron conduction
spot.intro: A rectangular conductor carries a current density $j_x>0$ in a field $\mathbf B=B\hat z$. The charge carriers are electrons ($q=-e$). Determine $E_y$ and $R_H$.
steps: Electrons drift opposite to the current: $\mathbf v_d=-v_d\hat x$ with $v_d=j_x/(ne)$.
Lorentz force $\mathbf F=q(\mathbf E+\mathbf v_d\times\mathbf B)$ pushes the electrons towards $-y$.
In steady state no net force acts in $y$: $\mathbf E+\mathbf v_d\times\mathbf B=0$ (the factor $q$ drops out).
$\mathbf v_d\times\mathbf B=(-v_d\hat x)\times B\hat z=+v_dB\hat y$, so $E_y=+v_dB$.
spot.why: The balance gives $\mathbf E=-\mathbf v_d\times\mathbf B$, so $E_y=-v_dB$ (the minus sign in step 3 was dropped). The electrons pile up at $-y$, so that side is negative and the field points towards $-y$.

source.where: adapted from Problem 2b (Hall effect), topic: sign of R_H

spot.title: Mean free path of electrons in copper
spot.intro: Copper at 300 K: $n=8.5\cdot10^{28}\,\text{m}^{-3}$, $\rho=1.7\cdot10^{-8}\,\Omega$m. Estimate relaxation time $\tau$ and mean free path $\ell$ using the Drude relation and Fermi-gas velocities.
steps: Speed of the conducting electrons: the classical thermal velocity $v=\sqrt{3k_BT/m}\approx1.17\cdot10^{5}$ m/s.
Result: about 10 lattice constants between collisions.
spot.why: Only electrons near $E_F$ carry current, with $v_F=\hbar k_F/m\approx1.57\cdot10^6$ m/s, about 10 times the classical thermal value (Pauli principle, Sommerfeld correction to Drude).

source.where: adapted from Problem 2b (Drude conductivity), topic: v_F vs v_thermal

spot.title: Intrinsic carrier density at 400 K versus 300 K
spot.intro: Silicon, $E_g=1.12$ eV. By which factor does the intrinsic carrier density $n_i$ increase from 300 K to 400 K (assume $E_g$ constant)?
steps: Mass-action law: $np=N_cN_v\,e^{-E_g/k_BT}$, and $n=p=n_i$ for the intrinsic case.
spot.why: Taking the square root of $np$ halves the exponent: $n_i\propto e^{-E_g/2k_BT}$. The activation energy of intrinsic carriers is $E_g/2$ (the chemical potential sits mid-gap).

source.where: adapted from the script, semiconductors chapter, topic: intrinsic carrier density

spot.title: Effective moment of Fe$^{3+}$
spot.intro: Fe$^{3+}$ has configuration $3d^5$. Using Hund's rules, find $S,L,J$ and the effective paramagnetic moment $p_{\rm eff}$ (in $\mu_B$).
steps: Hund 1: maximise $S$. Five electrons in five orbitals with parallel spin: $S=5/2$.
Hund 2: maximise $L$ compatible with it. Each $m_l=-2,\dots,2$ occurs once, so $L=\sum m_l=0$.
spot.why: The Curie constant contains $\langle\mu^2\rangle=g^2\mu_B^2J(J+1)$, so $p_{\rm eff}=g\sqrt{J(J+1)}$, not $gJ$. The latter would be the maximal projection of the moment.

source.where: adapted from the script, magnetism chapter, topic: Hund's rules and Curie law

spot.title: Degeneracy pressure of the free electron gas
spot.intro: Copper conduction electrons: $n=8.5\cdot10^{28}\,\text{m}^{-3}$, $E_F=7.0$ eV. Estimate the degeneracy pressure at $T=0$.
steps: Substituting numbers the shortcut $P=\tfrac23nE_F$ is used: $P\approx64$ GPa.
Same order as the bulk modulus of Cu (about 140 GPa): the gas pressure dominates the electronic part of the stiffness.
spot.why: In step 3 the factor $\tfrac35$ was kept, but then the number uses $\tfrac23 nE_F$, which is $2U/(3V)$ with $U/V=nE_F$ (forgetting that the mean energy is only $\tfrac35E_F$).

source.where: adapted from Problem 2a/2b (metal under pressure), topic: P = 2U/3V

spot.title: Effective mass at the bottom of a tight-binding band
spot.intro: 1D tight-binding chain, $E(k)=\varepsilon_0-2t\cos ka$ with $t=1$ eV and $a=3$ Å. Determine the effective mass at $k=0$ in units of $m_e$ ($\hbar^2/m_e=7.62$ eV Å$^2$).
spot.why: From $\hbar^2/(2m^*)=ta^2$ follows $m^*=\hbar^2/(2ta^2)$; the factor 2 stayed on the wrong side. Equivalent: $m^*=\hbar^2/(\partial^2E/\partial k^2)=\hbar^2/(2ta^2)$.

source.where: adapted from MC (n) tight-binding mass

limits.title: Debye heat capacity at low temperature
limits.prompt: How does the lattice heat capacity of an insulator behave for $T\ll\Theta_D$?
limits.explain: Only long-wavelength acoustic phonons with $\hbar\omega\lesssim k_BT$ are excited: the number of excited modes scales as $T^3$ (3D, $g(\omega)\propto\omega^2$) and each carries energy $\sim k_BT$, giving $C_V=\tfrac{12\pi^4}{5}Nk_B(T/\Theta_D)^3$. Option 4 is the Einstein result.

source.where: Ch. 2.3-2.4 (pp. 52-65), topic: Debye T^3 law

limits.title: Einstein model at low temperature
limits.prompt: In the Einstein model with frequency $\omega_E$, what is $C_V$ for $k_BT\ll\hbar\omega_E$?
limits.explain: A single mode of energy $\hbar\omega_E$ is frozen out exponentially: $C_V=3Nk_B(\Theta_E/T)^2e^{\Theta_E/T}/(e^{\Theta_E/T}-1)^2\to3Nk_B(\Theta_E/T)^2e^{-\Theta_E/T}$. This is why the Einstein model fails against the measured $T^3$ law.

source.where: MC (l) Einstein model

limits.title: Heat capacity at high temperature
limits.prompt: What value does $C_V$ of the Debye and the Einstein model approach for $T\gg\Theta$?
limits.explain: For $k_BT\gg\hbar\omega_{max}$ every one of the $3N$ oscillators contributes $k_B$ (equipartition: $\tfrac12k_BT$ kinetic plus $\tfrac12k_BT$ potential energy). Both models therefore share the Dulong-Petit value.

source.where: Ch. 2.3-2.4 (pp. 52-65), topic: classical limit of C_V

limits.title: Monatomic chain for small q
limits.prompt: For the monatomic chain $\omega(q)=2\sqrt{C/m}\,|\sin(qa/2)|$, what is the limit $q\to0$?
limits.explain: $\sin x\approx x$ gives $\omega\approx a\sqrt{C/m}\,|q|$, so $v=a\sqrt{C/m}$ equals the sound velocity of the elastic continuum. At the zone boundary $\omega_{max}=2\sqrt{C/m}$ with zero group velocity.

source.where: Ch. 2.2 (pp. 40-48), topic: monatomic chain

limits.title: Diatomic chain with equal masses
limits.prompt: In the diatomic chain take $m\to M$ (same atoms, same springs). What happens to the gap at $q=\pi/a$?
options: It closes; the dispersion folds back onto the monatomic one
The optical branch disappears, only the acoustic one remains in the extended zone
limits.explain: The gap is $\sqrt{2C}(1/\sqrt m-1/\sqrt M)$, which vanishes for $m=M$. The cell is then really half as large; the zone $[-\pi/a,\pi/a]$ is the monatomic zone folded in half (zone folding). Option 4 is a restatement of the same effect in the extended-zone picture, not a statement of what happens in the diatomic scheme.

source.where: Ch. 2.2.5 (pp. 45-48), topic: zone folding

limits.title: Drude conductivity at high frequency
limits.prompt: The Drude conductivity is $\sigma(\omega)=\sigma_0/(1-i\omega\tau)$. What is its limit for $\omega\tau\gg1$?
options: $\sigma\to0$ and the current is in phase with $E$
limits.explain: For $\omega\tau\gg1$ the electrons do not collide during one period, they simply accelerate: $m\dot v=-eE$ gives $j=i\,ne^2E/(m\omega)$, 90 degrees out of phase with $E$ (no dissipation). For $\omega\tau\ll1$ one recovers $\sigma_0=ne^2\tau/m$.

source.where: adapted from Problem 2b, topic: Drude AC conductivity

limits.title: Reflectivity of a metal around the plasma frequency
limits.prompt: With $\varepsilon(\omega)=1-\omega_p^2/\omega^2$ (undamped), how does an electromagnetic wave behave for $\omega>\omega_p$ and for $\omega<\omega_p$?
limits.explain: For $\omega>\omega_p$, $\varepsilon>0$ and the wavenumber $k=\sqrt\varepsilon\,\omega/c$ is real: the wave propagates. For $\omega<\omega_p$, $\varepsilon<0$, $k$ is imaginary and the wave is evanescent (reflected). Alkali metals become transparent in the UV.

source.where: adapted from Problem 2b, topic: plasma frequency

limits.title: Donor semiconductor at low temperature
limits.prompt: In an n-type semiconductor (donor density $N_d$, ionisation energy $E_d$) at very low temperature, how does the electron density depend on $T$?
limits.explain: At $k_BT\ll E_d$ the chemical potential lies midway between donor level and conduction band edge; with $n\approx\sqrt{N_cN_d/2}\,e^{-E_d/2k_BT}$ and $N_c\propto T^{3/2}$ one finds $T^{3/4}e^{-E_d/2k_BT}$. Option 2 is the exhaustion range at intermediate $T$, option 3 is intrinsic conduction at high $T$.

source.where: adapted from the script, doped semiconductors, topic: freeze-out

limits.title: Exhaustion range
limits.prompt: In the same semiconductor at intermediate temperature ($E_d\ll k_BT$ but $n_i\ll N_d$) what is $n$?
limits.explain: All donors are ionised, and thermally excited intrinsic carriers are still negligible: $n=N_d$. In this plateau the conductivity is governed by the temperature dependence of the mobility. At higher $T$ intrinsic carriers $n_i\propto e^{-E_g/2k_BT}$ take over.

source.where: adapted from the script, doped semiconductors, topic: exhaustion regime

limits.title: Hall coefficient of an intrinsic semiconductor
limits.prompt: For an intrinsic semiconductor with $n=p$, mobilities $\mu_e,\mu_h$: what is $R_H$?
limits.explain: Two-band formula $R_H=\dfrac{p\mu_h^2-n\mu_e^2}{e(p\mu_h+n\mu_e)^2}$ with $n=p$ yields option 1. Since $\mu_e>\mu_h$ in most semiconductors, $R_H<0$ (electron-like) even though both carriers exist.

source.where: adapted from Problem 2b, topic: Hall effect, two carrier types

limits.title: Fermi function far above the chemical potential
limits.prompt: What does the Fermi function $f(E)=1/(e^{(E-\mu)/k_BT}+1)$ approach for $E-\mu\gg k_BT$?
limits.explain: The exponential in the denominator dominates: $f\approx e^{-(E-\mu)/k_BT}$. This classical limit is applied for carriers in the conduction band of semiconductors. Exactly $f=\tfrac12$ holds only at $E=\mu$.

source.where: adapted from the script, Fermi-Dirac statistics

limits.title: Electronic heat capacity of a metal
limits.prompt: How does the electronic contribution to $C$ of a metal behave at low $T$, and what does $C/T$ against $T^2$ show?
options: $C=\gamma T+\beta T^3$, a straight line in $C/T$ versus $T^2$ with intercept $\gamma$
$C=\beta T^3$ only, the electrons don't contribute
limits.explain: Only electrons within $k_BT$ of $E_F$ can be excited (fraction $T/T_F$), so $C_{el}=\gamma T$ with $\gamma=\tfrac{\pi^2}{2}Nk_B/T_F$; phonons add $\beta T^3$. Plotting $C/T=\gamma+\beta T^2$ gives $\gamma$ and $\Theta_D$. The classical value $\tfrac32Nk_B$ is wrong by a factor $T/T_F\sim10^{-2}$.

source.where: adapted from the script, Sommerfeld theory, topic: electronic specific heat

limits.title: Density of states in different dimensions
limits.prompt: For free electrons ($E=\hbar^2k^2/2m$), which statement on $g(E)$ near $E\to0$ is correct?
limits.explain: $g(E)\propto k^{d-1}\,dk/dE\propto E^{(d-2)/2}$. Hence $E^{-1/2}$ in 1D (van Hove singularity at the band edge), constant $m/\pi\hbar^2$ per area in 2D, $\sqrt E$ in 3D.

source.where: MC (o) 2D DOS

limits.title: Metal under pressure
limits.prompt: A free-electron metal is compressed to half its volume at fixed electron number. By which factor does $E_F$ change?
limits.explain: $E_F\propto n^{2/3}\propto V^{-2/3}$. Halving $V$ doubles $n$ and multiplies $E_F$ by $2^{2/3}$. Note that the exponent 2/3 holds for 3D; in 2D $E_F\propto n$.

source.where: adapted from Problems 2a/2b (Aug 2024), metal under pressure

limits.title: Curie-Weiss susceptibility near $T_C$
limits.prompt: $\chi=C/(T-T_C)$ above the Curie temperature of a ferromagnet. What happens for $T\to T_C^+$ and for $T\gg T_C$?
options: Diverges at $T_C$; for $T\gg T_C$ reduces to Curie law $\chi\approx C/T$
Vanishes at $T_C$; Curie law for $T\gg T_C$
limits.explain: In the molecular-field picture the internal exchange field enhances the response, so $\chi\to\infty$ as $T\to T_C^+$ (onset of spontaneous magnetisation). For $T\gg T_C$ the shift in the denominator is negligible and the Curie law of free moments is recovered.

source.where: adapted from the script, magnetism chapter, topic: Curie-Weiss law

limits.title: Resistivity of a metal at low and high T
limits.prompt: How does the ideal (phonon) resistivity of a metal vary for $T\ll\Theta_D$ and $T\gg\Theta_D$ (Bloch-Gruneisen)?
options: Constant in both limits, only the impurity term $\rho_0$ matters
limits.explain: At high $T$ the number of phonons is $\propto T$ and each scatters equally, so $\rho\propto T$. At low $T$ fewer phonons ($T^3$) and small-angle scattering (an extra factor $T^2$) give $T^5$. Matthiessen: $\rho=\rho_0+\rho_{ph}(T)$, with the constant residual $\rho_0$ from impurities.

source.where: adapted from Problem 2b, topic: Matthiessen rule and rho(T)

limits.title: Degenerate matter: dependence of pressure on density
limits.prompt: For a 3D degenerate non-relativistic electron gas at $T=0$, how does $P$ depend on density $n$, and what changes in the ultra-relativistic limit?
limits.explain: NR: $P=\tfrac25nE_F\propto n\cdot n^{2/3}$. UR: $E=\hbar ck$, $E_F\propto n^{1/3}$ and $P=\tfrac13nE_F\propto n^{4/3}$. The softer $n^{4/3}$ equation of state leads to the Chandrasekhar mass limit.

source.where: adapted from the script, free electron gas, topic: degeneracy pressure (cross-region boss)

sketch.title: Phonon dispersion of the diatomic chain
sketch.task: Sketch $\omega(q)$ for a linear chain of alternating masses $m<M$ with spring constant $C$ over the first Brillouin zone (positive $q$ only). Mark band edges and the gap.
features: Acoustic branch starts linearly, $\omega=vq$, from 0 (slope = sound velocity).
Optical branch starts at $\sqrt{2C(1/m+1/M)}$ at $q=0$ and decreases with zero slope.
At $q=\pi/a$: $\omega_{ac}=\sqrt{2C/M}$ (lower) and $\omega_{opt}=\sqrt{2C/m}$ (upper), both with zero group velocity.
A frequency gap exists between the branches, closing for $m=M$.
Both branches have horizontal tangents at the zone boundary.
sketch.tips: Mark the three special frequencies on the $\omega$ axis before drawing curves.

source.where: Ch. 2.2.5 (pp. 45-48), topic: diatomic chain

sketch.title: Debye versus Einstein heat capacity
sketch.task: Sketch $C_V/(3Nk_B)$ against $T/\Theta$ for the Debye model and for the Einstein model (take $\Theta_E=0.75\,\Theta_D$ and plot against $T/\Theta_D$). Indicate the limits.
features: Both curves tend to 1 (Dulong-Petit) at high $T$.
Debye: $C_V\propto T^3$ at low $T$ (cubic rise).
Einstein: exponentially small at low $T$, below the Debye curve there.
Debye reaches about 95% of the classical value at $T\approx\Theta_D$.
Both curves start at 0 for $T\to0$ (third law).
sketch.tips: Einstein: $C=3Nk_B x^2e^x/(e^x-1)^2$ with $x=\Theta_E/T$; Debye: integral up to $x_D=\Theta_D/T$.

source.where: Ch. 2.3-2.4 (pp. 52-65), topic: Debye and Einstein models

sketch.title: 3D free-electron DOS and electron distribution
sketch.task: Sketch the free-electron density of states $g(E)$ and the occupied density $g(E)f(E)$ at $k_BT=0.1E_F$ and at $T=0$ against $E/E_F$.
features: $g\propto\sqrt E$ rises with infinite slope at $E=0$.
At $T=0$ the occupied part ends sharply at $E_F$ (step).
At finite $T$ the step is smeared over a width of a few $k_BT$ around $\mu$.
$\mu$ is slightly lower than $E_F$ (by $\tfrac{\pi^2}{12}(k_BT)^2/E_F$) because $g$ rises with $E$.
The number of electrons (area under $gf$) is the same as at $T=0$.

source.where: adapted from the script, Sommerfeld theory

sketch.title: Resistivity versus temperature (Matthiessen)
sketch.task: Sketch $\rho(T)$ of a metal with impurities and of a purer sample of the same metal, up to $2\Theta_D$. Indicate the low- and high-$T$ regimes.
features: Both curves tend to the residual resistivity $\rho_0$ as $T\to0$.
The $T$-dependent part is identical (Matthiessen's rule): the curves are shifted by $\Delta\rho_0$.
Low $T$: $\rho-\rho_0\propto T^5$ (very flat).
High $T$ ($T\gtrsim\Theta_D$): linear in $T$.
Crossover near $T\approx\Theta_D/4$ to $\Theta_D/2$.

source.where: adapted from Problem 2b, topic: Matthiessen rule and rho(T)

sketch.title: 1D tight-binding band
sketch.task: Sketch $E(k)=\varepsilon_0-2t\cos ka$ for $0\le k\le\pi/a$ (set $\varepsilon_0=0$, energies in units of $t$) and add the parabola of the effective-mass approximation at the band bottom.
features: Band bottom $E=-2t$ at $k=0$, band top $E=+2t$ at $k=\pi/a$; bandwidth $4t$.
Zero slope at $k=0$ and at the zone boundary $k=\pi/a$.
Parabola agrees with the band for small $k$ and lies above it afterwards.
Inflection point at $ka=\pi/2$ where $m^*$ changes sign (effective mass diverges).
Negative effective mass in the upper half (holes at the band top).

source.where: adapted from MC (n) tight-binding mass

sketch.title: Fermi function at several temperatures
sketch.task: Sketch $f(E)=1/(e^{(E-\mu)/k_BT}+1)$ for $T=0$, and for $k_BT=0.02\mu$ and $0.1\mu$, against $E/\mu$.
features: All curves pass through $f=1/2$ at $E=\mu$.
T=0 is a step function; the smearing region is of width $\approx\pm2k_BT$.
The curves are point-symmetric about $(\mu,\tfrac12)$: $f(\mu+\delta)=1-f(\mu-\delta)$.
For $E-\mu\gg k_BT$ the tail is Boltzmann-like.
Slope at $\mu$ is $-1/4k_BT$.

source.where: adapted from the script, Fermi-Dirac statistics

sketch.title: Carrier density of a doped semiconductor
sketch.task: Sketch $n(T)$ on a logarithmic scale against $1000/T$ for an n-type semiconductor ($N_d=10^{16}$ cm$^{-3}$, $E_d=50$ meV below the band edge, $E_g=1.12$ eV). Label the three regimes.
features: High $T$ (small $1000/T$): intrinsic, slope given by $E_g/2$.
Plateau $n\approx N_d$ (exhaustion) at intermediate $T$.
Low $T$: freeze-out with slope $E_d/2$ (flatter than intrinsic slope).
Intrinsic and doped curves merge at high $T$ and the plateau lies at $10^{16}$.
Slopes on this plot are $-E_a/k_B$ (Arrhenius).
sketch.tips: Think of three Arrhenius lines: $E_g/2$, plateau (slope 0), $E_d/2$.

source.where: adapted from the script, doped semiconductors

sketch.title: Inverse susceptibility versus temperature
sketch.task: Sketch $1/\chi(T)$ for a paramagnet, a ferromagnet with $T_C=100$ K and an antiferromagnet with $\Theta=-50$ K (in units $C=1$), for $T>0$ in the paramagnetic phase.
features: Paramagnet: straight line through the origin (Curie law).
Ferromagnet: parallel line shifted to the right, intercept at $T_C$, valid only for $T>T_C$.
Antiferromagnet: parallel line shifted left, intercept at negative $\Theta$ (and the Neel point lies above 0).
All three have the same slope $1/C$ at high $T$.
Intercept with the $T$ axis gives sign and size of the exchange interaction.

source.where: adapted from the script, magnetism chapter, topic: Curie-Weiss law

sketch.title: 1D phonon DOS: chain versus Debye
sketch.task: Sketch the phonon density of states of the monatomic chain, $g(\omega)\propto1/\sqrt{\omega_m^2-\omega^2}$, and compare with the Debye approximation of the same chain (same sound velocity and same number of modes).
features: Chain: $g(\omega)=\tfrac{2}{\pi}(\omega_m^2-\omega^2)^{-1/2}$, minimum $2/\pi$ at $\omega=0$.
Van Hove singularity (diverges) at $\omega_m$ where the group velocity vanishes.
Zero for $\omega>\omega_m$.
Debye (1D): constant, cut off at $\omega_D=\tfrac\pi2\omega_m$, larger than the true maximum.
Both match for $\omega\to0$ (same sound velocity).

source.where: Ch. 2.3 (pp. 52-65), topic: phonon DOS, van Hove singularity

sketch.title: Nearly free electrons: band gap at the zone boundary
sketch.task: Sketch the free-electron parabola $E=\hbar^2k^2/2m$ (extended zone) and the two lowest bands of the nearly-free-electron model in the reduced zone, showing the gap opening at $k=\pi/a$.
features: Free parabola reaches the zone boundary $k=\pi/a$ with $E=\hbar^2\pi^2/2ma^2$.
Bragg reflection at $k=\pi/a$ mixes $e^{ikx}$ and $e^{i(k-G)x}$, forming standing waves.
A gap $E_g=2|V_G|$ opens at the boundary: lower band flattens (zero slope), upper band starts flat.
Away from the boundary the bands follow the free-electron parabola (bands folded back).
The lower band edge sits at $E\approx-0.04$, slightly below the free value due to level repulsion with $k-G$.

source.where: adapted from Task 5 (M-point gap), topic: nearly free electron model
